package screen

import (
	"strings"

	"github.com/pkar/pvim/internal/text"
	"github.com/pkar/pvim/internal/window"
)

// One window's text area, drawn a buffer line at a time.
//
// Every rule in here is a screen dump of vim 9.2.0321 taken through
// screenchar() with :set lines= and :set columns=, not a reading of the
// documentation. Where the two disagreed the dump won; where a dump could not
// be taken the comment says so.

// winCtx is the state of drawing one window: everything the row loop needs,
// resolved once so the inner loop does no option lookups.
type winCtx struct {
	f   *Frame
	s   *Screen
	w   *window.Window
	g   Groups
	fld *Folds

	// text is where the buffer's own characters go, which is the window
	// rectangle less its status line and less the 'number' column.
	text Region
	// numWidth is the width of the 'number' column, 0 when 'number' is off.
	numWidth int

	tabstop     int
	wrap        bool
	lineBreak   bool
	breakIndent bool
	breakAt     string
	showBreak   string
	leftCol     int
	cursorLine  bool

	current bool
}

// drawText paints the window's buffer lines, the fold lines that stand in for
// them, and the '~' rows past the end of the buffer.
func (c *winCtx) drawText() {
	b := c.w.Buf
	if b == nil {
		b = text.New()
	}
	last := b.LineCount()

	row := c.text.Row
	end := c.text.Row + c.text.Rows
	lnum := c.w.View.TopLine
	if lnum < 1 {
		lnum = 1
	}

	shown := c.w.View.TopLine
	if shown < 1 {
		shown = 1
	}
	// shown is the last line the window showed the whole of, which is what
	// vim's w_botline counts and what line('w$') reports. A line that needed
	// more rows than were left is not one of them: measured on vim 9.2.0321 at
	// 40x8 with 'wrap', a buffer of "a" to "e" and a hundred x's answers
	// line('w$') 5, and the ruler says Top rather than All. The exception is
	// the top line itself, which vim counts however little of it fits, because
	// w_botline is never below w_topline + 1: a 300-character line alone in
	// the same window answers 1.
	for row < end && lnum <= last {
		if fold := c.fld.ClosedAt(lnum); fold != nil {
			c.drawFold(row, fold)
			row++
			shown = fold.End
			lnum = fold.End + 1
			continue
		}
		used, fits := c.drawLine(row, end, lnum, b.Line(lnum))
		row += used
		if !fits {
			break
		}
		shown = lnum
		lnum++
	}

	c.f.noteBotLine(c.w.ID, min(shown, last))

	// Past the end of the buffer: the 'eob' item of 'fillchars', which is '~',
	// in EndOfBuffer. Vim paints the whole row in that highlight and not only
	// the one cell, which shows up the moment a colourscheme gives the group a
	// background.
	eob := c.fillChar("eob", '~')
	for ; row < end; row++ {
		c.s.Grid.Fill(row, c.text.Col-c.numWidth, c.numWidth+c.text.Cols, ' ', c.g.EndOfBuffer)
		if eob != 0 {
			c.s.Grid.Set(row, c.text.Col-c.numWidth, eob, c.g.EndOfBuffer)
		}
	}
}

// drawLine paints one buffer line starting at row, using as many rows as
// 'wrap' needs, and returns how many it used.
//
// The second result is false when the line needed more rows than were left.
// What happens then is 'display', and vim does three different things:
//
//	display=truncate   as many rows as fit less one, then "@@@" on the last
//	display=lastline   every row that fits, with "@@@" over its last three cells
//	display=           the line is not drawn at all and every leftover row
//	                   gets a single "@" in its first column
//
// Measured on a 20-column window six rows tall over "aaa", "bbb" and a
// hundred x's. vim's own defaults.vim sets truncate, so that is what --clean
// does and what the oracle compares against.
func (c *winCtx) drawLine(row, end, lnum int, line []byte) (int, bool) {
	segs := c.segments(line)
	if !c.wrap {
		c.drawSegment(row, lnum, line, segs[0], false)
		return 1, true
	}
	if row+len(segs) <= end {
		for i, seg := range segs {
			c.drawSegment(row+i, lnum, line, seg, i > 0)
		}
		return len(segs), true
	}

	at := c.fillChar("lastline", '@')
	col := c.text.Col - c.numWidth
	width := c.numWidth + c.text.Cols

	switch {
	case strings.Contains(c.f.Display, "truncate"):
		for i := 0; row+i < end-1; i++ {
			c.drawSegment(row+i, lnum, line, segs[i], i > 0)
		}
		c.s.Grid.Fill(end-1, col, width, ' ', c.g.NonText)
		c.s.Grid.Fill(end-1, col, 3, at, c.g.NonText)
	case strings.Contains(c.f.Display, "lastline"):
		for i := 0; row+i < end; i++ {
			c.drawSegment(row+i, lnum, line, segs[i], i > 0)
		}
		c.s.Grid.Fill(end-1, col+width-3, 3, at, c.g.NonText)
	default:
		for r := row; r < end; r++ {
			c.s.Grid.Fill(r, col, width, ' ', c.g.NonText)
			c.s.Grid.Set(r, col, at, c.g.NonText)
		}
	}
	return end - row, false
}

// drawFold paints the one row a closed fold occupies.
func (c *winCtx) drawFold(row int, fold *Fold) {
	c.drawNumber(row, fold.Start, false)
	txt := FoldText(c.w.Buf, fold, c.fld.LevelAt(fold.Start))
	col := c.s.Grid.SetString(row, c.text.Col, txt, c.g.Folded)
	fill := c.fillChar("fold", '-')
	c.s.Grid.Fill(row, col, c.text.Col+c.text.Cols-col, fill, c.g.Folded)
	if c.current && c.cursor().Line >= fold.Start && c.cursor().Line <= fold.End {
		c.s.CursorRow, c.s.CursorCol = row, c.text.Col
	}
}

// drawNumber paints the 'number' column for one screen row. wrapped rows get
// blanks, which is vim with 'cpoptions' free of "n".
func (c *winCtx) drawNumber(row, lnum int, wrapped bool) {
	if c.numWidth == 0 {
		return
	}
	col := c.text.Col - c.numWidth
	hl := c.g.LineNr
	if c.cursorLine && lnum == c.w.View.Cursor.Line {
		hl = c.g.CursorLineNr
	}
	c.s.Grid.Fill(row, col, c.numWidth, ' ', hl)
	if wrapped {
		return
	}
	s := itoa(lnum)
	if len(s) > c.numWidth-1 {
		s = s[len(s)-(c.numWidth-1):]
	}
	c.s.Grid.SetString(row, col+c.numWidth-1-len(s), s, hl)
}

// segment is one screen row's worth of a buffer line: the characters on it and
// the number of cells of indent in front of them.
type segment struct {
	chars  []Char
	indent int

	// start is the display column of the row's first text cell, counted from
	// the left edge of the line. It is not chars[0].Col: a tab split across
	// the wrap boundary belongs to two rows and starts before the second one
	// does.
	start int

	// arrow marks a row that ended because the next character was too wide
	// for the cell or cells left over. Vim puts a ">" in them rather than
	// leaving them blank, under 'wrap' as well as under 'nowrap'.
	arrow bool
}

// segments splits a line into the rows it occupies.
//
// Under 'nowrap' there is always exactly one, holding every character, and the
// row loop clips it against LeftCol. Under 'wrap' the split honours
// 'breakindent' and 'linebreak', both measured against vim:
//
//	:set wrap breakindent, columns=30, "    alpha beta ... kappa"
//	    alpha beta gamma delta eps
//	    ilon zeta eta theta iota k
//	    appa
//
//	:set wrap breakindent linebreak
//	    alpha beta gamma delta
//	    epsilon zeta eta theta
//	    iota kappa
func (c *winCtx) segments(line []byte) []segment {
	chars := Chars(line, c.tabstop)
	if !c.wrap || len(chars) == 0 {
		// An empty line is one empty row, wrapped or not. Without this the
		// loop below has no character to make progress on and walks off the
		// end of the slice.
		return []segment{{chars: chars}}
	}

	width := c.text.Cols
	if width < 1 {
		width = 1
	}
	indent := c.continuationIndent(line, width)

	var out []segment
	i := 0
	col := 0 // display column this row's text starts at
	for {
		avail := width
		if len(out) > 0 {
			avail = width - indent
		}
		if avail < 1 {
			avail = 1
		}
		start := i
		at := col // display column reached so far on this row
		lastBreak := -1
		for i < len(chars) {
			if chars[i].Col+chars[i].Width > col+avail {
				break
			}
			at = chars[i].Col + chars[i].Width
			if c.lineBreak && c.isBreakAt(chars[i]) {
				lastBreak = i
			}
			i++
		}
		arrow, split := false, false
		switch {
		case i == start && i < len(chars) && chars[i].Tab:
			// A tab wider than the whole row. Vim fills the row with it and
			// carries the rest onto the next: at 'tabstop' 16 in a 12-column
			// window a leading tab leaves the first row blank and four more
			// cells of it on the second.
			split = true
		case i == start:
			// One character wider than the whole row. It has to go somewhere,
			// so it goes here and the row overflows into nothing.
			i++
		case c.lineBreak && i < len(chars) && lastBreak >= start && lastBreak+1 < i:
			i = lastBreak + 1
		case i < len(chars) && at < col+avail && chars[i].Tab:
			// A tab straddling the right edge is split, and only a tab is:
			// vim puts the cells before the edge on this row and the rest at
			// the start of the next, so every display column after it carries
			// straight across. Measured at 12 columns, 'tabstop' 8, over
			// "aaaaaaaaaa<Tab>Zbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb":
			//
			//	aaaaaaaaaa
			//	    Zbbbbbbb
			//	bbbbbbbb
			split = true
		case i < len(chars) && at < col+avail && chars[i].Width > 1:
			arrow = true
		}

		seg := segment{start: col, arrow: arrow}
		if split {
			// The tab is on both rows: this one draws the cells up to the
			// edge and the next one draws the rest, each clipped by drawChar.
			seg.chars = chars[start : i+1]
		} else {
			seg.chars = chars[start:i]
		}
		if len(out) > 0 {
			seg.indent = indent
		}
		out = append(out, seg)

		if split {
			col += avail
			continue
		}
		if i >= len(chars) {
			return out
		}
		col = chars[i].Col
	}
}

// isBreakAt reports whether a character is one 'linebreak' may break after.
func (c *winCtx) isBreakAt(ch Char) bool {
	if ch.Tab {
		return strings.ContainsRune(c.breakAt, '\t')
	}
	if ch.Text != "" {
		return false
	}
	return strings.ContainsRune(c.breakAt, ch.Rune)
}

// continuationIndent is how far in a 'breakindent' continuation row starts.
//
// Vim's rule with 'breakindentopt' empty: the line's own indent, but never so
// far that fewer than 20 cells of text are left. That floor is
// 'breakindentopt' min:20, which nothing in this editor changes.
func (c *winCtx) continuationIndent(line []byte, width int) int {
	if !c.breakIndent {
		return 0
	}
	n := 0
	for _, b := range line {
		switch b {
		case ' ':
			n++
		case '\t':
			n += c.tabstop - n%c.tabstop
		default:
			return capIndent(n, width)
		}
	}
	return capIndent(n, width)
}

// capIndent applies 'breakindentopt' min:20 to a computed indent.
func capIndent(n, width int) int {
	if max := width - 20; n > max {
		n = max
	}
	if n < 0 {
		n = 0
	}
	return n
}

// drawSegment paints one screen row of one buffer line.
func (c *winCtx) drawSegment(row, lnum int, line []byte, seg segment, cont bool) {
	c.drawNumber(row, lnum, cont)

	base := c.g.Normal()
	if c.cursorLine && lnum == c.w.View.Cursor.Line {
		base = c.g.CursorLine
	}
	c.s.Grid.Fill(row, c.text.Col, c.text.Cols, ' ', base)

	left := c.text.Col
	right := left + c.text.Cols
	off := 0 // cells of the row already used
	if cont {
		off = seg.indent
		if c.showBreak != "" {
			off = c.s.Grid.SetString(row, left+off, c.showBreak, c.g.NonText) - left
		}
	}

	// Under 'nowrap' the row shows the line from LeftCol; under 'wrap' the
	// segment already starts where the row does.
	origin := 0
	if !c.wrap {
		origin = c.leftCol
	} else {
		origin = seg.start - off
	}

	cursorOnLine := c.current && c.cursor().Line == lnum
	matches := c.matchesOn(lnum)

	if seg.arrow && len(seg.chars) > 0 {
		last := seg.chars[len(seg.chars)-1]
		if x := left + last.Col + last.Width - origin; x < right {
			c.s.Grid.Fill(row, x, right-x, '>', c.g.NonText)
		}
	}

	for _, ch := range seg.chars {
		x := left + ch.Col - origin
		if x+ch.Width <= left {
			continue
		}
		if x >= right {
			break
		}
		hl := base
		if id, ok := matchHL(matches, ch.Byte, ch.Size); ok {
			hl = id
		}
		if cursorOnLine && c.cursorIn(ch) {
			c.s.CursorRow, c.s.CursorCol = row, clampCol(x, left, right-1)
		}
		c.drawChar(row, x, left, right, ch, hl)
	}

	// The cell after the last byte of the line, which is the newline. Two
	// different things land on it.
	//
	// A cursor past the last byte sits there, which is where insert mode
	// leaves it and where an empty line puts it.
	//
	// A match whose End runs past the last byte highlights it, which is what
	// makes a linewise Visual selection on a short line look different from a
	// charwise one that stopped at the end of the text, and is the only way an
	// empty line inside a selection shows at all. Measured on vim 9.2.0321 at
	// 20 columns over "abc", an empty line and "ijk", reading screenattr() per
	// cell: "Vjj" highlights four cells on row 1 and one on row 2, while "v$"
	// on the same first line highlights three. There is no byte past the last
	// one to hang a Char on, so it cannot come out of the loop above.
	if lastSegment(line, seg) {
		x := left
		if n := len(seg.chars); n > 0 {
			last := seg.chars[n-1]
			x = left + last.Col + last.Width - origin
		}
		if hl, ok := matchHL(matches, len(line), 1); ok && x >= left && x < right {
			c.s.Grid.Set(row, x, ' ', hl)
		}
		if cursorOnLine && c.cursor().Col >= len(line) {
			c.s.CursorRow, c.s.CursorCol = row, clampCol(x, left, right-1)
		}
	}
}

// lastSegment reports whether a segment holds the end of its line, which is
// where a cursor past the last byte belongs.
func lastSegment(line []byte, seg segment) bool {
	if len(seg.chars) == 0 {
		return len(line) == 0
	}
	last := seg.chars[len(seg.chars)-1]
	return last.Byte+last.Size >= len(line)
}

// drawChar puts one character's cells on the row, clipped to left..right.
//
// The two clipped cases are vim's, both measured on a 12-column screen under
// 'nowrap' over "ab" followed by CJK runes, scrolled a column at a time with
// zl:
//
//	b一二三四五>     leftcol 1: the rune at the right edge becomes ">"
//	<二三四五六>     leftcol 3: the rune split by the left edge becomes "<"
func (c *winCtx) drawChar(row, x, left, right int, ch Char, hl HLID) {
	switch {
	case ch.Tab:
		n := ch.Width
		if x < left {
			n -= left - x
			x = left
		}
		if x+n > right {
			n = right - x
		}
		c.s.Grid.Fill(row, x, n, ' ', hl)
	case ch.Text != "":
		for _, r := range ch.Text {
			if x >= left && x < right {
				c.s.Grid.Set(row, x, r, hl)
			}
			x++
		}
	case x < left:
		c.s.Grid.Fill(row, left, x+ch.Width-left, '<', c.g.NonText)
	case x+ch.Width > right:
		// A double-width rune that will not fit in the cells left is not
		// drawn: vim puts a '>' in the last column instead. Measured on a
		// 12-column screen with "abcdefghijk" then a CJK rune, under both
		// 'wrap' and 'nowrap':
		//
		//	abcdefghijk>
		c.s.Grid.Set(row, x, '>', c.g.NonText)
	default:
		c.s.Grid.Set(row, x, ch.Rune, hl)
	}
}

// cursorIn reports whether the window's cursor byte falls in this character.
func (c *winCtx) cursorIn(ch Char) bool {
	col := c.cursor().Col
	return col >= ch.Byte && col < ch.Byte+ch.Size
}

// cursor is where the caret goes: the window's own cursor, unless the frame
// has moved it for one redraw, which is what 'showmatch' does.
func (c *winCtx) cursor() text.Pos {
	if c.f.CursorOver != nil {
		return *c.f.CursorOver
	}
	return c.w.View.Cursor
}

// matchesOn gathers every highlighted byte range on a line, in the order the
// later ones win: 'hlsearch' first, then the 'incsearch' preview, then the
// visual selection on top.
func (c *winCtx) matchesOn(lnum int) []hlRange {
	var out []hlRange
	if c.f.Search != nil {
		for _, m := range c.f.Search.MatchesOn(lnum) {
			out = append(out, hlRange{m.Start, m.End, c.g.Search})
		}
	}
	if m := c.f.IncSearch; m != nil && m.Line == lnum {
		out = append(out, hlRange{m.Start, m.End, c.g.IncSearch})
	}
	if c.f.Visual != nil {
		for _, m := range c.f.Visual.MatchesOn(lnum) {
			out = append(out, hlRange{m.Start, m.End, c.g.Visual})
		}
	}
	return out
}

// hlRange is a byte range on one line and the highlight it carries.
type hlRange struct {
	start, end int
	hl         HLID
}

// matchHL returns the highlight covering a character, if any. A character is
// covered when any of its bytes are, which is what puts every cell of a tab in
// the Search highlight when a match runs across it:
//
//	:set hlsearch tabstop=4, /ab\tcd over "zz ab<Tab>cd zz"
//	zz ab   cd zz
//	...aaaaaaa...   (a = Search)
func matchHL(ranges []hlRange, byteAt, size int) (HLID, bool) {
	found, ok := HLID(0), false
	for _, r := range ranges {
		if byteAt < r.end && byteAt+size > r.start {
			found, ok = r.hl, true
		}
	}
	return found, ok
}

// clampCol keeps a cursor cell inside the window. The high end wins when the
// window is so narrow that there is no room between the two, because a cell
// past the right-hand edge is off the grid and one before the left is only
// off the text area.
func clampCol(x, lo, hi int) int {
	if x < lo {
		x = lo
	}
	if x > hi {
		x = hi
	}
	return x
}

// Normal is the id every un-highlighted cell carries, spelled as a method so
// that drawing code reads the same whichever group it is asking for.
func (g Groups) Normal() HLID { return HLID(0) }

// fillChar returns one item of 'fillchars', or def when it is not set.
func (c *winCtx) fillChar(item string, def rune) rune {
	return fillChar(c.f.opts().G.FillChars, item, def)
}

// fillChar parses one item out of a 'fillchars' string.
func fillChar(spec, item string, def rune) rune {
	for _, part := range strings.Split(spec, ",") {
		name, val, ok := strings.Cut(part, ":")
		if !ok || name != item {
			continue
		}
		for _, r := range val {
			return r
		}
	}
	return def
}

// itoa is strconv.Itoa for a non-negative line number, here so the hot row
// loop does not reach for a package for three digits.
func itoa(n int) string {
	if n == 0 {
		return "0"
	}
	neg := n < 0
	if neg {
		n = -n
	}
	var b [20]byte
	i := len(b)
	for n > 0 {
		i--
		b[i] = byte('0' + n%10)
		n /= 10
	}
	if neg {
		i--
		b[i] = '-'
	}
	return string(b[i:])
}
